theme: Oh how I love your law; your word is a lamp
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 119:97-120. This section of the great psalm on God’s word speaks of love for the law, sweetness, and light for the path. Read verse 105 slowly.
settingTheScene: Psalm 119 is the longest chapter in the Bible, an acrostic of twenty-two stanzas, each beginning with a successive letter of the Hebrew alphabet. In this plan, it is spread across several days. Today’s reading covers three stanzas, Mem, Nun, and Samekh, and speaks of the power of God’s word. Jesus said that his word would make us free, and this psalm shows the heart that treasures it.
observation: “Oh how I love your law! It is my meditation all the day” (v. 97).
“Your commandment makes me wiser than my enemies, for it is ever with me” (v. 98).
“How sweet are your words to my taste, sweeter than honey to my mouth!” (v. 103).
“Through your precepts I get understanding; therefore I hate every false way” (v. 104).
“Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path” (v. 105).
“You are my hiding place and my shield; I hope in your word” (v. 114).
“Hold me up, that I may be safe and have regard for your statutes continually!” (v. 117).
“My flesh trembles for fear of you, and I am afraid of your judgments” (v. 120).
interpretation:
The stanza called Mem begins with an exclamation of love: “Oh how I love your law!” The psalmist is not describing a duty but a delight. He meditates on God’s word all day, and it makes him wiser than his enemies, wiser than his teachers, and wiser than the aged. It gives him wisdom because it comes from God and it shapes his conduct. He keeps his feet from every evil way. Then comes the sweetness: “How sweet are your words to my taste, sweeter than honey to my mouth!”

The next stanza, Nun, begins with the best-known line: “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path.” A lamp in the ancient world did not light up the whole road. It showed the next step. God’s word may not tell us everything about the future, but it shows us enough to take the next step. The psalmist has sworn to keep God’s righteous rules, and he is deeply afflicted, yet he says, “Give me life, O LORD, according to your word.” The word is both light and life. He asks that the LORD accept his freewill offerings of praise, and says that God’s testimonies are the joy of his heart.

In Samekh, the psalmist hates the double-minded and loves God’s law. “You are my hiding place and my shield; I hope in your word.” Here the word is not just a lamp but a shelter. He asks for help to keep the commandments and for God to uphold him: “Hold me up, that I may be safe.” He knows that on his own he cannot stand. The stanza ends with fear and trembling: “My flesh trembles for fear of you.” A right fear of God does not exclude love; it deepens it.

In John, Jesus is the Word, and he said, “If you abide in my word, you are truly my disciples.” To love God’s word is to love him. Jesus Christ fulfilled the law the psalmist loved, and the Spirit he sends writes it on our hearts.
connection: Psalm 1:2 and 19:7-11 also praise the delight of the law. Joshua 1:8 commands meditation on the book of the law. Jeremiah 15:16 says your words became to me a joy. Matthew 4:4 quotes Deuteronomy 8:3, that man lives by every word from God’s mouth. John 8:31-32 and 17:17 speak of the truth of the word. 2 Timothy 3:16-17 says all Scripture is breathed out by God. Hebrews 4:12 says the word of God is living and active.
application:
Read verse 105 aloud and ask what the next step is for you. Where do you need light?

Choose a short passage and meditate on it throughout the day, as verse 97 describes.

Ask God to make his word sweeter to you than honey. Pray it honestly.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what you love about his law.
Ask him to let it be your meditation all the day.
Ask him to light your path with it.
